Low-level design — thiết kế class và viết ra code

Vòng LLD nằm giữa DSA và system design: không hỏi thuật toán khó, cũng không vẽ kiến trúc trên mây, mà bắt bạn chia class và viết code chạy được trong 45 phút. Rakuten, Grab, Agoda và phần lớn công ty Nhật/global đều có vòng này.
Low-level design — designing the classes and writing the code

The LLD round sits between DSA and system design: no hard algorithms, no architecture in the clouds — just split the classes and write working code in 45 minutes. Rakuten, Grab, Agoda and most Japanese and global companies run this round.

How does a low-level design interview differ from system design, and what five-step framework should you use?

System design (HLD)Low-level design (LLD)
Unitservice, database, queue, cacheclass, interface, method
Focusscale, consistency, partitioningresponsibilities, coupling, extensibility
Deliverablediagram + trade-offsworking code
Follow-up"What happens at 10× traffic?""How many places change when type X is added?"
**Five-step framework (a communication and invariant workflow; timeboxes are adjustable):** 1. **Clarify the scope** — LLD prompts are deliberately ambiguous: *"Elevator: how many cars? Priority floors? Scheduling only, or a full simulation?"* Agree on the smallest scope, actors, and success invariants that fit the interview; three to five minutes is a useful example, not a ritual. 2. **List use cases** — identify what each actor can do. These become the methods later. 3. **Identify entities and responsibilities** — nouns become classes and verbs become methods. State explicitly: *"This class has the single responsibility of…"* 4. **Sketch the API before implementing it** — write method signatures and interfaces, [[g:confirm them]], then fill in method bodies. Avoid writing 40 lines before discovering that the prompt was misunderstood. 5. **Code the core** — implement the most interesting part as working code; describe repetitive parts as *"analogous"* and move on. :::tip What the interviewer actually evaluates The [[o:extensibility of the design]]. A common follow-up is *"What if we add another vehicle, fee, or strategy type?"* If the answer is "add one class implementing the existing interface", the design is easy to extend. If it is "edit the `switch` in three places", the design has a change hotspot. ::: :::deep - [[r:do not draw an ERD]]. LLD asks for the in-memory *object* model, not a schema. Jumping to tables and foreign keys immediately leaves the problem's scope. - begin with interfaces and enums, and defer storage; an in-memory `Map` is more than enough unless the prompt says otherwise - state the system [[g:invariants]], such as *"a seat cannot be both FREE and HELD"*, then show where the code enforces them. This distinguishes a senior from a mid-level answer. - prefer [[o:composition over inheritance]]: a deep inheritance tree signals immature design. A four-level `Car extends Vehicle` hierarchy for a "vehicle types" problem almost always has a better composition-based alternative. - manage time with a heuristic: reserve enough time for a working core, then adjust clarification, design, coding, and extension discussion to the prompt. [[r:Running out of time without working code]] is the worst outcome, so implement the core early. - always ask *"Does this need to be thread-safe?"* If yes, explain the strategy (22-low-level-design-ood.patterns-in-interview-code.q3); if no, mention that concurrency was considered. :::

Take-home brief: a Q&A REST service where users ask questions, answer open ones, and up- or down-vote both. How do you keep the score right under concurrent votes, and how do you scope three days?

**Read the brief as a contract.** Create questions, list open ones, answer, vote ±1 on questions and answers; tags and sign-up are optional. CRUD is not the hard part — a vote is *one per user per post*, and the score must agree with the votes. **API:** 
POST   /questions                    {title, body, tags[]}    → 201 + Location
GET    /questions?status=open&tag=java&cursor=…                → one page
POST   /questions/{id}/answers       {body}                   → 201
PUT    /posts/{id}/vote              {"value": 1 | -1}        → 200 {score, myVote}
DELETE /posts/{id}/vote                                       → 200 {score, myVote: 0}
`PUT` because a vote is *the state of my vote*, not an event: sending it twice is harmless, so a retry is safe without an idempotency key (17-rest-api-design.contracts-errors-lifecycle.q1). Questions and answers share a `post` table with a `kind`, so a vote has one foreign key. **The constraint is the rule, and a changed vote moves the score by the difference** (+1 to −1 is −2): 
CREATE TABLE vote (
  post_id bigint   NOT NULL REFERENCES post,
  user_id bigint   NOT NULL,
  value   smallint NOT NULL CHECK (value IN (-1, 1)),
  PRIMARY KEY (post_id, user_id)            -- one vote per user per post
);
──── one transaction; PostgreSQL 18 returns the old value from the upsert
INSERT INTO vote VALUES ($1, $2, $3)
ON CONFLICT (post_id, user_id) DO UPDATE SET value = EXCLUDED.value
RETURNING COALESCE(old.value, 0) AS before;    -- old.* is NULL on a fresh insert
UPDATE post SET score = score + ($3 - :before) WHERE id = $1;   -- relative: no lost update
On an older PostgreSQL or on MySQL, start the transaction with `SELECT … FROM post WHERE id = ? FOR UPDATE`: votes on one post then serialize, and reading the old vote is safe. **Scope three days by risk, not by feature count:** 1. day one: the vote path end to end, with a test that fires 50 concurrent votes and asserts `score = SUM(value)`. 2. day two: questions, answers and the open list with cursor pagination. 3. day three: `docker compose up` that starts the app and the database with migrations, plus a README listing every assumption. Tags and auth come last. :::tip What reviewers read first The vote invariant and its test, the README's assumptions, and whether `docker compose up` works on a clean machine. Feature count comes after all three. ::: :::deep - **stored score or computed?** `SUM(value)` over an index on `vote(post_id)` is exact and needs no update path; a stored `score` makes "sort by score" an index scan. Store it only when listing by score is required, and keep a reconciliation query that recomputes it. - the relative `score = score + delta` is the point: read-modify-write in Java (`post.setScore(post.getScore() + 1)`) loses votes under concurrency unless the row is locked or versioned (05-db-core-index-lock.transactions-mvcc-locking.q3). - per tier: at T1–T3 serializing the votes of one post on its row costs nothing anyone notices; at T4 a viral post is a hot row that `needs its own scaling story` — votes appended as events, the score folded asynchronously and shown as approximate (25-microservice.06-hot-partition-db-bottleneck.q1). - rules to state as assumptions: no voting on your own post (enforce in the service and answer with a problem-details error), whether closed questions accept votes, and whether a deleted post keeps its votes. - "open" needs a definition — no accepted answer, or not closed by a moderator. Write it down, index `(status, created_at)` for the list, and page with a cursor (17-rest-api-design.contracts-errors-lifecycle.q5). - RFC 9457 error bodies, validation at the controller boundary and Flyway owning the schema make a take-home read like production code (17-rest-api-design.contracts-errors-lifecycle.q2). - the same shape — a uniqueness constraint as the rule, a relative counter as the projection — answers likes, follows and reactions in a system-design round. :::
How do you reference SOLID naturally in an LLD interview without sounding formulaic?

Reciting the five letters from memory is [[r:counterproductive]]. Use them correctly by reaching a design decision, [[g:naming the relevant principle, and immediately moving on]].

- [[b:S]] — Single Responsibility. *"I separated `PricingStrategy` because its reason to change differs from `ParkingLot`."* The rule is "one reason to change", not "one method".
- [[b:O]] — Open/Closed. *"Adding a new vehicle type means adding an implementation, not editing existing classes."* This is often useful to demonstrate in an extension question.
- [[b:L]] — Liskov. A subtype must replace its base type without violating expectations. The classic `Square extends Rectangle` fails because `setWidth` also changes the height.
- [[b:I]] — Interface Segregation. Interfaces should be small and consumer-specific. A 20-method `Repository` forces every implementation to provide all 20 methods.
- [[b:D]] — Dependency Inversion. `ParkingLot` depends on the `PricingStrategy` abstraction, not the concrete `WeekendPricing`.

:::tip A strong interview line
*"I apply Open/Closed [[o:where I expect change]]—the pricing calculation. I keep unlikely-to-change areas simple because premature abstraction is also debt."* Explaining a principle's **limits** is what sounds senior.
:::

:::deep
- the [[r:over-engineering trap]] is creating an interface for every class "to follow SOLID". An interface with one implementation that will never gain a second is [[o:noise]], not good design. YAGNI wins until a real axis of change appears.
- Dependency Inversion is not Dependency Injection. DI is a common *mechanism* for achieving DIP; confusing the concepts is a frequent interview mistake.
- SRP correctly means *"group things that change for the same reason and separate things that change for different reasons"*. It is based on **who or what requests the change**, not the number of tasks a class performs.
- a common real-world Liskov violation is a subclass throwing `UnsupportedOperationException`, as with `Collections.unmodifiableList`. Recognizing that even standard libraries violate the rule shows understanding rather than memorisation.
- SOLID arose around inheritance-heavy OOP; modern design leans toward [[o:composition, pure functions, and immutable data]]. Mentioning that perspective demonstrates maturity.
- combine other principles naturally: DRY, while avoiding merging coincidentally similar code, KISS, YAGNI, and the Law of Demeter
:::
When should you choose Strategy, State, or Chain of Responsibility?

The three patterns look similar because all of them plug in behavior, but they answer three different questions.
Change axisPreferSignal
Algorithm/rule changesStrategysame lifecycle, different way to do the work
Lifecycle/state changesStatelegal behavior follows the current state
Request routingChainhandlers may accept or forward
No real change axisplain class/functionan extra pattern would be over-engineering
PatternAnswersWho chooses the next behavior
Strategyhow should it be done? — interchangeable algorithmsthe client chooses; it does not change mid-operation
Statewhere are we now? — behavior changes with statethe current state transitions to the next state
Chainwho handles it? — try handlers in sequence until one acceptseach handler decides whether to handle or forward
**Strategy** — pricing, compression choice, or scheduling algorithm: 
lot = new ParkingLot(new WeekendPricing());   // injected at construction
**State** — booking lifecycle, vending machine, or order: 
interface BookingState {
    BookingState pay(Booking b);       // return the next state
    BookingState cancel(Booking b);
}
//
class Held implements BookingState {
    public BookingState pay(Booking b) { b.charge(); return new Paid(); }
    public BookingState cancel(Booking b) { b.releaseSeat(); return new Cancelled(); }
}
The benefit is that [[g:invalid transitions become impossible]]: `Cancelled.pay()` can simply throw an error, with no scattered `if` statements. **Chain of Responsibility** — middleware, filters, or validation pipelines: 
auth.setNext(rateLimit).setNext(validate).setNext(handler);
:::deep - the signal for State is [[r:the same `if (status == ...)` chain repeated across several methods]]. That is a state machine hidden inside `if` statements. - State [[o:holds context]] and transitions itself; Strategy is [[o:stateless]] and selected externally. It is a useful distinction when the lifecycle, not just the algorithm, changes. - in modern Java, a Strategy is often just a [[g:lambda]] (`Function`/`Predicate`) rather than a class hierarchy. Saying so shows understanding rather than pattern worship. - an `enum` can implement State compactly in Java by overriding methods per constant, especially when states hold no private data - a long Chain is [[r:difficult to debug]]; add logs or traces at every link and define whether an unhandled input is an error or is silently ignored - patterns commonly paired in LLD include [[o:Factory]] (construct the correct type from input), [[o:Observer]] (notify changes), [[o:Builder]] (objects with many optional arguments), and [[o:Command]] (undo/redo or queued tasks) - [[r:do not force patterns]] into a design to show them off. A misplaced pattern is worse than none; the interviewer will ask *"Why is it needed here?"*, and the answer must be real. :::
What thread-safety questions arise in an LLD interview, and how should you answer them?

Almost every LLD problem ends with *"What if multiple threads call it concurrently?"* A prepared framework makes the answer quick. **Four levels, in preferred order:** 1. [[g:Immutability]] — no shared mutable state means no concurrency problem. Mention this first. 2. [[g:Single-thread confinement]] — funnel work through a queue to one coordinator thread, as in an elevator or actor model. 3. [[g:Concurrent data structures]] — `ConcurrentHashMap`, `AtomicLong`, and `BlockingQueue`. These are sufficient for most problems. 4. [[g:Explicit locking]] — `synchronized` or `ReentrantLock`. This is the most powerful and the easiest to get wrong. **The common interviewer trap** is a compound operation on `ConcurrentHashMap`: 
// WRONG: each call is atomic, but the PAIR is not
if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v);
//
// CORRECT: one atomic operation
map.putIfAbsent(k, v);
map.computeIfAbsent(k, key -> new Spot(key));
*"Using `ConcurrentHashMap` makes it safe"* is [[r:incorrect]]. It guarantees individual operations, not sequences of operations. **A correct parking-space allocation example:** 
public Optional<Spot> allocate(Vehicle v) {
    Queue<Spot> free = freeByType.get(v.requiredSpot());
    Spot s = free.poll();                  // ConcurrentLinkedQueue: atomic poll
    return Optional.ofNullable(s);         // one vehicle = one spot, no lock required
}
:::deep - [[o:minimize lock scope]]: lock an individual spot or key rather than the entire lot. Using `synchronized` on every method of a singleton serializes the entire system. - consistent lock ordering is the cheapest deadlock prevention: when two locks are needed, always acquire them by increasing ID (see 5.10 and 23.3) - `ReentrantLock` versus `synchronized`: the former provides `tryLock(timeout)`, interruptible acquisition, and multiple `Condition`s (23-java-concurrency-coding.classic-synchronisation-problems.q1). Without those requirements, `synchronized` is simpler and well optimized by the JIT. - [[r:do not]] make outbound HTTP or database calls while holding a lock; doing so lengthens the critical section and increases deadlock risk - for read-heavy, write-light workloads, use `ReadWriteLock`, or copy-on-write when writes are extremely rare (23-java-concurrency-coding.classic-synchronisation-problems.q4) - a useful knowledge check: [[o:`volatile`]] guarantees *visibility*, not *atomicity*. `volatile int i; i++` is still broken. This is a classic follow-up question. - if the prompt does not require concurrency, say *"I will design the single-threaded version first for clarity, then identify the synchronisation points."* Raising it proactively is better than waiting to be challenged. :::

How do you design an object model for testability, invariants, and deterministic concurrency tests?

Testability is an architectural property. Keep domain decisions in small objects or pure functions; put clocks, randomness, ID generation, persistence, messaging, and scheduling behind narrow injected ports. This lets tests control inputs without exposing private fields or adding production-only switches. 
interface Clock { Instant now(); }
interface IdSource { String next(); }
final class HoldService {
    private final Clock clock;
    private final HoldRepository holds;
    // constructor injection; no Instant.now() hidden in domain logic
}
Express each aggregate invariant and legal transition close to the state it protects: a hold cannot expire before creation, a released hold cannot be confirmed, balance-changing commands must preserve the ledger equation. Return explicit outcomes instead of using exceptions for every expected rejection. Make side effects occur after a decision through ports, and define idempotency where commands can be retried. Use a layered test portfolio: - [[b:Example/unit tests]] cover boundaries and state transitions with a fake clock and deterministic IDs. - [[b:Property/model-based tests]] generate command sequences and assert invariants after every step; a simple reference model can catch optimized-implementation mistakes. - [[b:Contract/integration tests]] verify adapters against the real database, broker, serializer, or HTTP contract. - [[b:Concurrency tests]] first identify the linearization point, then coordinate targeted interleavings with barriers/latches and bounded timeouts. Add sustained stress or OpenJDK jcstress as exploratory stress evidence for Java Memory Model questions; a passing run is evidence, not proof. :::deep Do not use `Thread.sleep` as synchronization. Inject virtual time for TTL and refill logic; use explicit signals to know when a worker reached the intended point. Record seeds and shrink failing property cases. Assert final state and externally visible history, not implementation timing. Thread safety is part of the public contract: document which methods are safe concurrently, compound-operation semantics, callback/reentrancy rules, fairness, blocking, cancellation, and ownership of returned mutable data. Prefer designs with a single owner or immutable snapshots when they make illegal interleavings unrepresentable. The concurrency reasoning framework is covered in (16-project-concurrency-whiteboard.technical-storytelling-fundamentals.q3). :::
What must a correct in-memory TTL cache specify beyond O(1) get and put?

O(1) lookup is only the data-structure part. A correct TTL cache needs an explicit contract for time, visibility, cleanup, replacement, capacity, restart and concurrency.
DecisionSafe default to discussFailure if omitted
Expiration timeStore an absolute deadline; use an injected monotonic elapsed-time source for in-process expiryWall-clock jumps make entries live too long or expire early
Read semantics`get` checks the deadline and treats expired data as a missExpired data is returned until a background thread happens to clean it
CleanupLazy cleanup plus bounded scheduled/eviction work; cleanup is not validityExpired keys leak memory or a cleanup scan creates latency spikes
Replacement raceVersion/generation or compare-and-remove when deleting an expired entryOld cleanup deletes a newer value written for the same key
Restart/distributionState whether data is disposable and process-local; use a shared authority only when the contract needs itA local cache is mistaken for a lock, source of truth, or cross-instance rate limit
:::deep - `java.time.Clock` is injectable but represents wall-clock time. For elapsed TTL in one process, inject a monotonic ticker backed by `System.nanoTime`; for persisted/distributed deadlines, define clock-skew and absolute-time behavior explicitly. - ConcurrentHashMap makes individual map operations safe, not the whole `get-or-refresh`, `put-if-newer`, or stale-cleanup workflow. Use `compute`, a lock/actor, or a versioned compare-and-remove around the invariant. - A timer is an optimization. Correctness must remain true if cleanup is delayed, duplicated, reordered, or stopped. - In Redis or another shared cache, TTL/eviction/replication are provider contracts; they do not automatically provide fencing, durable truth or business idempotency. Link distributed leases to Topic 28 and API semantics to Topic 17. - Tests should advance a fake ticker, race expiry against replacement, restart the process, bound memory, and verify metrics for hit/miss/expired/evicted/stale-cleanup outcomes. :::

What should a team's coding conventions actually enforce — and which rules belong in a tool rather than a review comment?

Conventions exist so a reviewer spends attention on design, not on spacing. That splits them in two. **Mechanical — a tool fails the build and nobody argues in review:** - formatting: one formatter (google-java-format through Spotless, or a checked-in IDE profile), run on commit and in CI. - style a parser can see: Checkstyle with a shared config, Google's or Sun's as the base. - bug patterns: Error Prone; nullness through JSpecify annotations checked by NullAway — the annotations Spring Framework 7 and Boot 4 adopted. **Judgement — written down once, applied in review:**
RuleGoodWhy
names say purpose, not formFILE_PATH_SEPARATOR = "/"
not SLASH		the value may change; the meaning should not
booleans read as a questionisActive · hasOrders() · canCheckout()if (order.canCheckout()) reads as a sentence
one verb per actalways findBy…, never also get… or select… for the same lookupa synonym makes the reader hunt for a difference
domain words in codethe term the business usesthe ubiquitous language (24-domain-driven-design.strategic-splitting-the-domain.q1)
**Null is a design decision, not a check sprinkled everywhere.** Decide which values may be absent, mark them, and validate at the boundary. `Optional` belongs on return types — the JDK's own note calls it "primarily intended for use as a method return type" — not on fields, parameters or collections. 
Optional<Customer> findByEmail(String email);       // absence is a real answer
List<Order> ordersOf(CustomerId id);                 // empty list, never null
void notify(Optional<String> channel)              // use an overload or a default
if (!ObjectUtils.isEmpty(x)) x.run();             // hides why x could be null
:::tip The test for a convention If a tool can check it, automate it; if it needs judgement, write the reason beside the rule. A rule with no reason gets broken by the next person who has one. ::: :::deep - "never a `for` loop, always streams" is a dogma to drop: streams win for transform-filter-collect pipelines; a loop is clearer with an early exit, checked exceptions or index arithmetic. Choose per case, and keep side effects out of `map` and `filter`. - a [[g:first-class collection]] — a class wrapping one collection with the behaviour on it (`Orders.totalPaid()`) — gives that behaviour one home; worth it once the same filtering appears in three places. - getters only where a caller needs them, and no setters on domain objects: behaviour lives on the object, rather than data pulled out and decided elsewhere — the anemic model (12-architecture-patterns.patterns-principles.q3). - "a method does one thing" is about one level of abstraction, not a line count; a long `if/else` over a type is a strategy, or a `switch` over a sealed type, waiting to happen (12-architecture-patterns.patterns-principles.q7). - a constant lives next to its only user (`private static final`); a project-wide `Constants` class becomes a junk drawer that every module depends on. - comments explain *why* — a decision, a constraint, a workaround and its ticket. A comment that repeats the code goes stale the first time the code changes. - a quality gate in CI (Sonar, Checkstyle) works only if a red gate blocks the merge; a gate people merge past teaches them to ignore it. :::
